transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to see me?

Well, I suppose I'm here because... it really comes down to the project files at work. I'm a translator and interpreter, you see. For months now, I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern in our system. And you know, recognizing patterns is basically my entire job. I actually did my graduate degree in applied linguistics, focusing on syntax variations. It’s fascinating how language structures evolve. I spent a whole summer in Prague during my studies just doing field research. Beautiful city, really. The architecture is incredible, especially near the river. I used to go to this tiny bakery every morning that made these amazing plum pastries. I’ve tried baking them at home since then, but I can never get the dough quite right. My oven runs a bit hot, I think, or maybe it's the humidity here, it just completely changes how the yeast behaves. 

But anyway, where was I? Right, the files. So, certain subcontractors and this one specific colleague of mine, they keep making these tiny, almost invisible changes to the translation memory and the timestamps. It’s very subtle. Translation memory is the database we use—it remembers past translations to keep things consistent. I remember when we first transitioned to this new cloud-based software, what a complete headache that was. Half the office couldn't figure out the interface, and I had to spend three days walking everyone through the new shortcut keys. 

But yeah, they're going in and altering the timestamps so it looks like my quality control failed on these projects. I even took it to IT, and of course, IT says the audit trail is totally clean. But I know what I'm looking at. The record has been deliberately arranged to put the blame on me.

You mentioned IT checked the audit trail and said it was clean. When you look back at the specific evidence that convinced you the files were altered—apart from what IT found—what exactly do you see that proves someone changed them?

Well, like I was saying, it’s just... you can see the record has been deliberately arranged to put the blame on me. Even when IT looks at it and says the audit trail is completely clean, I know what I'm looking at. The evidence is in those tiny changes to the translation memory. And the timestamps, of course. 

Speaking of timestamps, it actually gets incredibly complicated with the time zones, because we have subcontractors all over the place. I was working with this one subcontractor in Tokyo last year. Or maybe it was Osaka? No, it was definitely Tokyo, because he sent me this amazing picture of the cherry blossoms near Ueno Park. I’ve always wanted to go to Japan in the spring. I actually started learning a bit of Japanese on my commute just to prepare for a trip someday. Just the basics, you know, hiragana and katakana. 

But the commute is just brutal these days. I take the bus sometimes, but when I drive, it's a nightmare. They’ve been doing construction on the interstate for what feels like three years now. I had to get my car's alignment checked twice last month because of the potholes. The mechanic tried to upsell me on new brake pads, but I know a thing or two about cars. My dad used to rebuild old Mustangs in our garage when I was a kid. He had this gorgeous '67 fastback... cherry red. We used to spend every Sunday afternoon just tinkering under the hood. He always said if you listen closely, the engine will tell you exactly what's wrong with it. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Right, the files. The subcontractors and that one colleague. They keep making those little changes to the memory so it looks like my quality control failed. It's all right there in the pattern, no matter what IT says.
Have you ever seen things or heard voices that other people around you couldn't see or hear, or experienced anything like that?

No, no, nothing like that. I don't hear voices or see things that aren't there. My hearing is actually quite good, though. Better than most people's, I think. I took this online frequency test a few months ago, and I can still hear the pitches they say you're supposed to lose by the time you're thirty. It's probably because I've always been careful about wearing earplugs at concerts. 

I used to go to a lot of live music when I was in grad school. There was this one jazz club downtown—just a tiny, basement place, barely had room for a trio—but they brought in the most incredible musicians. I saw this saxophone player there once, and he did this twenty-minute solo that just... it was mesmerizing. I actually tried to learn the sax for a little while after that. Rented one from a shop near my apartment. But the reed kept drying out on me, and honestly, the noise complaints from my neighbors started getting a bit aggressive. The walls in that building were paper-thin. You could hear the guy next door every time he sneezed. He had this terrible allergies, always sneezing. 

But no, to answer your question, I don't hear voices or anything. Just the normal sounds. And, of course, the people at work talking, but that's just normal office chatter.

When did you first start noticing these changes to the files and becoming concerned that your colleagues were altering them? Was it something that happened suddenly over days or weeks, or has this been building up gradually over months?

Well, let's see... it’s been going on for about 11 months now. It started shortly after I was put in charge of this massive new localization project we landed. We were adapting the interface for a new line of smart home appliances for the European market. Which is actually a fascinating challenge, because the length of words in German compared to English completely breaks the user interface layout if you aren't careful. I had to have so many meetings with the design team about text expansion. 

The lead designer on that, this guy named Marcus, he was absolutely obsessed with the typography. He insisted on using this one specific sans-serif font—Helvetica Neue, I think it was. People get really passionate about fonts, you know? There's actually this whole documentary I watched a few years ago just about the history of Helvetica. It's amazing how a typeface can completely change the psychological impact of a message. I started paying attention to all the street signs after watching that. Like, the highway signs around here use a font called Highway Gothic, but I noticed they’ve been slowly replacing it with Clearview on the newer overpasses. Though I read an article recently saying the transportation department might be switching back to the old one because of visibility issues at night. Night driving is getting harder for me anyway, honestly. The glare from those new LED headlights on oncoming cars is just completely blinding. I had to buy special yellow-tinted glasses just to drive home from the grocery store after dark. 

But... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, the timeline. Yeah, about 11 months ago, right after that localization project kicked off, that's when I first started seeing the discrepancies in the files.

You mentioned this started about 11 months ago after the localization project. Before that project began, did you ever have concerns that colleagues were tampering with your work or altering files—or is this something that only started happening around that time?

No, before the smart home project, things were completely fine. I was mostly working on this huge batch of technical manuals for a company that manufactures agricultural equipment. Combines, tractors, that sort of thing. It's incredibly dense material, lots of highly specific terminology about hydraulics and threshing mechanisms. I actually had to buy a specialized physical dictionary just for agricultural engineering terms because the online glossaries were so unreliable. 

I love physical dictionaries, actually. The smell of the paper. I have this whole collection of vintage dictionaries in my home office. My favorite is this massive 1913 Webster's Unabridged. It weighs something like fifteen pounds. It's got these beautiful marbled endpapers. You just don't see bookbinding like that anymore, you know? Everything now is just cheap glue that cracks after a year. It's a real shame. I took a bookbinding workshop once on a weekend just to see how they used to do it with the stitching and the leather. We had to use these specialized awls to punch the holes, and I ended up pricking my thumb so badly I couldn't type properly for a week. 

Which is a complete disaster when you're a translator paid by the word, let me tell you. I had to try using speech-to-text software while my thumb healed, and the mistakes it made were just hilarious. It kept translating "hydraulic valve" as "hideous vault." I spent more time correcting the software than I would have just typing with nine fingers. 

But... wait, what was the question? Oh, right, the tampering. No, before that localization project started 11 months ago, I never had any issues like that. I trusted my colleagues completely back then. It really just started with that specific project.

In the weeks or month right before you first noticed these file changes 11 months ago, did you experience any major stress at work, any significant life changes, or did you notice any changes in your mood, sleep, or how you were feeling in general?

Stress? Um, no, not really. I mean, work was busy, but just the normal kind of busy. No big life changes or anything. I was sleeping fine. Actually, I had just bought this amazing new mattress right around then. Memory foam, but with this cooling gel layer on top. I used to wake up sweating all the time, especially in the summer. My apartment gets terrible afternoon sun, just bakes the whole living room. 

I tried putting up those blackout curtains, the really heavy velvet ones? But they collect so much dust. I feel like I was constantly taking them down to wash them, and they weigh a ton when they're wet. I had to drape them over the shower rod to dry because they'd break the drying rack. And then the shower rod actually did come crashing down one morning while I was brushing my teeth. Scared the living daylights out of me. It chipped the porcelain on the edge of the bathtub, which I still need to get fixed. I called my landlord about it, but he's practically useless. He's this older guy who spends half the year in Florida, so getting him to send a maintenance person takes an act of Congress. 

He did finally send this plumber once to fix a leaky faucet in the kitchen, and the guy tracked mud all over my rug. It's a Persian rug, hand-knotted. I found it at an estate sale a few years ago. The amount of work that goes into making those rugs is just staggering. They can take months, sometimes years, to finish a single piece. I watched a video about the natural dyes they use—madder root for red, indigo for blue. It's a whole art form that's slowly dying out because of machine manufacturing. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, stress before the project. Right. No, no major stress or mood changes or anything like that. Everything was perfectly normal before all this started.

When you first started noticing these changes to the files 11 months ago, did the whole thing become clear to you pretty much right away—like you suddenly realized what was happening—or did it gradually dawn on you over days or weeks as you noticed more and more pieces of the pattern?

Well, it was definitely gradual. I didn't just wake up one morning and think, "Aha, they're sabotaging me." It was more like... I'd notice a small typo here, a formatting error there. At first, I just thought I was getting careless. I actually went out and bought a new pair of reading glasses because I thought maybe my eyes were just getting tired from staring at the screen so much. 

I got them from this little boutique optometrist downtown. They had this incredible selection of frames, mostly European designers. I ended up getting these tortoiseshell ones from Italy. The guy working there was telling me about how true tortoiseshell used to be made from actual sea turtles, which is just horrible when you think about it. Thank goodness they use acetate now. Acetate is actually a really fascinating material, it's made from wood pulp and cotton fibers, so it's technically a bioplastic. 

I've been trying to reduce my plastic use lately, actually. I switched to those bamboo toothbrushes, but honestly, the bristles are just too stiff. My dentist told me I was brushing too hard and wearing down my enamel. Enamel doesn't grow back, you know. Once it's gone, it's gone. That's why I stopped drinking sparkling water, too. The carbonic acid is terrible for your teeth. I used to drink three or four cans of that flavored seltzer a day. Black cherry was my favorite. I tried making my own with one of those carbonator machines, but the flavor syrups you buy at the store always taste so artificial, like cough medicine. 

Wait, sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, right, how I figured it out. Yeah, it wasn't a sudden realization. It took a few weeks of noticing those little changes before the pattern really started to click and I realized it wasn't just me making mistakes.

When IT checked the audit trail and told you it was completely clean, how did that make you feel about their conclusion? Do you think they might have missed something, or do you think they might be involved in covering this up?

When IT told me the audit trail was clean, I just... I knew they were wrong. Because for months I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern in the project files. It's always certain subcontractors and this one specific colleague. They keep making these tiny, microscopic changes to the translation memory and the timestamps, specifically so it looks like my quality control failed. 

Timestamps are so finicky anyway, you know? Did you know that server time can actually drift if it's not constantly synced to an atomic clock? I went down a huge rabbit hole reading about atomic clocks a few years ago. The cesium fountains they use to measure the exact second are just incredible. It completely changed how I look at timekeeping. I actually wear a mechanical watch, an old Omega Seamaster that I inherited from my uncle. It loses about four seconds a day, which used to drive me absolutely crazy until I learned how complex the escapement mechanism inside it is. You have to take it in every five years to get the synthetic oils replaced, otherwise the friction just grinds the little gears down to dust. The guy who services mine is this older Swiss watchmaker who works out of a tiny shop downtown that always smells like brass polish and peppermint. He wears these incredible magnifying loupes attached right to his glasses so he can see the jewels...

Sorry, I'm rambling about watches. What were you asking? Oh, right, IT and the audit trail. Yeah, so when IT says the audit trail is completely clean, it doesn't mean nothing happened. It just means the record has been deliberately arranged to put the blame on me. They covered their tracks, and IT is just looking at the fake history they left behind.

I want to understand this more clearly. You've mentioned several times that the files show evidence of tampering, but when I ask you what exactly proves it, you keep describing the pattern itself rather than specific details. Can you walk me through one concrete example—one specific file or timestamp change—that you've actually examined and that proves to you someone altered it?

A concrete example? Yeah, absolutely. If you look at the Spanish localization project we did last quarter... specifically the Castilian Spanish files, not the Latin American ones. The dialect differences are actually fascinating. Like, in Spain they use the 'vosotros' form, which you almost never hear in Mexico or Colombia. I spent a semester in Madrid during grad school, actually. The lifestyle there is just... so different. People eat dinner at, like, 10 PM. I remember going out for tapas and having the most incredible jamón ibérico. It's cured for up to four years, and the pigs only eat acorns. The flavor is just unbelievable. 

I tried buying some at a specialty deli here once, but it cost an absolute fortune. Like, a hundred dollars for just a few paper-thin slices. The guy behind the counter was using this beautiful, ultra-thin slicing knife. I actually bought a set of Japanese chef knives recently. High-carbon steel. You have to hand-wash them and oil them immediately or they rust, which is a bit of a pain, but they cut through a tomato like it's warm butter. I tried sharpening them on a whetstone last weekend and completely scratched the side of the blade...

Um, wait. Why was I talking about knives? Oh, right, the specific file. Well, the thing is, I’m here because for months I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern across all the project files, not just one isolated document. It’s always certain subcontractors and this one specific colleague. They keep making these tiny, deliberate changes to the translation memory and the timestamps. They do it specifically so it looks like my quality control failed. So when you ask for one concrete example, it's hard to just point to one line of code because it's systemic. And even when IT says the audit trail is completely clean, I know the record has been arranged to put the blame on me. They just manipulated the history before IT even looked at it.

I understand you see a pattern across the files. But let me ask you this directly: if you were to show me one specific file right now—just one—with a timestamp or a translation entry that you believe was altered, what would I be looking at, and what would tell me it was changed rather than just being a mistake you made?

If I showed you a file right now... well, if I pulled up the translation software, you'd be looking at the segment grid. I actually use a specialized dual-monitor setup for it so I can keep the source text on the left and the translation memory on the right. I just upgraded my monitors to these 4K IPS panels. The color accuracy is unbelievable. I had to recalibrate them using this little colorimeter tool because out of the box, the blues were way too saturated. 

I used to do a bit of amateur photography, mostly black and white film, so I'm really picky about contrast. Developing film in a darkroom is such a dying art, you know? The smell of the stop bath and the fixer... it takes me right back to college. I had this old Leica camera that weighed an absolute ton. Built like a tank. I ended up selling it to help pay for my master's degree, which I really regret now because vintage camera prices have absolutely skyrocketed over the last few years. I saw one at an antique shop last week going for... 

Wait, sorry, I completely lost my train of thought. You wanted to know what you'd see in the file that proves it wasn't my mistake. 

Look, I know I keep saying the same thing, but it's because you're asking for a smoking gun in a single document, and that's just not how they operate. What you'd be looking at is the culmination of what I've been seeing for months. It's that one specific colleague and those subcontractors making these tiny, calculated adjustments to the translation memory and the timestamps. They're doing it specifically to make it look like my quality control is slipping. And I know IT told you the audit trail is clean, but like I said before, I know for a fact the record has been arranged to put the blame on me. They scrubbed the real history. Looking at one isolated file won't show you the sabotage, because they've manipulated the whole system to make it look like my error.

If someone you trust completely—say, a family member or a close friend outside of work—looked at these files with you and told you they didn't see any evidence of tampering, is there any possibility they could be right, or are you certain that what you're seeing is real regardless of what they might conclude?

If someone I trust completely looked at them... like my brother, maybe? He's actually an accountant, so he's used to looking at spreadsheets and data all day. Though his kind of data is totally different. He works for this mid-sized firm that handles logistics companies. The whole supply chain industry is fascinating right now. During the pandemic, the cost of shipping a single container from Shanghai to Los Angeles went from like two thousand dollars to over twenty thousand. Can you imagine? I read this whole book about container ships recently. They're massive. The engines are the size of a small apartment building, and they run on this thick, sludgy bunker fuel that you actually have to heat up before you can even pump it into the engine. It's terrible for the environment, but they're experimenting with methanol and ammonia now to try and make it greener. I actually saw a documentary about a ship that got stuck in the Suez Canal...

Wait, sorry. You asked if my brother looked at the files and didn't see anything, would I think he was right. 

No. No, I wouldn't. Because he doesn't know what to look for. Even if he's smart, he doesn't know the system. Like I've been saying, I'm here because for months I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern in the project files. It's always those certain subcontractors and that one colleague. They keep making these tiny, deliberate changes to the translation memory and the timestamps specifically so it looks like my quality control failed. It's so subtle that an outsider wouldn't catch it. And even when IT says the audit trail is completely clean, I know the record has been deliberately arranged to put the blame on me. They wouldn't leave obvious clues for a friend or family member to find. The tampering is real, regardless of who else can see it.
You've mentioned 'that one specific colleague' several times. Can you tell me their name and describe exactly what you believe their motive is for tampering with your files?

His name? It's David. David from the localization team. As for his motive... well, he's always been incredibly ambitious, you know? He actually started out in marketing before moving to localization. Marketing is such a weird field. My cousin works in digital marketing, doing SEO optimization for e-commerce sites. She says the Google algorithm changes so often that half her job is just trying to guess what the search engine wants this week. She used to work for this startup that sold artisanal pet food. Like, organic, grain-free kibble made from wild-caught salmon and sweet potatoes. People spend an absolute fortune on their pets these days. I saw a dog stroller at the park the other day that looked more expensive than my first car. It had shock absorbers and everything. I mean, I love dogs, I grew up with a golden retriever named Buster who was the sweetest thing, but a stroller? 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, David. Right. 

Look, I don't know exactly what his grand plan is, but I've told you why I'm here. For months, I've been seeing the exact same pattern in the project files. It's David and those specific subcontractors. They keep making these tiny, deliberate changes to the translation memory and the timestamps. They're doing it specifically so it looks like my quality control failed, maybe so he can take over my projects or push me out. And I know I keep repeating myself, but even when IT says the audit trail is completely clean, I know for a fact the record has been arranged to put the blame on me. He's just covering his tracks.
Have you brought this concern to your supervisor or to HR at your company, and if so, what did they say when you showed them the evidence of the tampering?

I did go to my supervisor, and I actually set up a meeting with HR last month. HR is on the third floor now since they renovated the building. They switched the entire office to an open-plan layout, which is just absolutely awful for concentration, especially when you're translating complex technical documents. I had to buy these incredibly expensive noise-canceling headphones just to hear myself think. The Sony ones, you know? The battery life on them is fantastic. I listen to a lot of history podcasts while I work, mostly about the Roman Empire. Did you know that the Romans actually had a surprisingly complex system of indoor plumbing? They used lead pipes, which obviously wasn't great for their health in the long run, but the engineering was brilliant for the time. Aqueducts are just fascinating. I visited the Pont du Gard in southern France a few years ago, and standing under those arches... 

Wait, sorry. I'm doing it again. You asked what HR and my supervisor said. 

Well, they didn't believe me. They just parroted what IT said about the audit trails. I mean, I haven’t lost my job or missed any major deadlines or anything like that. But things are definitely different now. Project meetings have become really tense because I keep pressing for the record to be corrected, and they just want to sweep it under the rug. It's gotten to the point where a few colleagues now avoid looping me into routine discussions unless they absolutely have to. They're just freezing me out because I won't drop it.

Have you shown these files or discussed the specific evidence of tampering with anyone outside of work—a family member, a close friend, or maybe another professional like an accountant or lawyer—and what did they think when you explained what you were seeing?

Show the files to someone outside of work? No, no, I haven't done that. I haven't talked to a lawyer or anything. For one thing, we have very strict NDAs—non-disclosure agreements. As a translator, you sign them constantly because you're often dealing with sensitive, pre-release material. 

I translated a massive batch of patents last year for this Japanese tech firm, actually. They were designing a new type of induction rice cooker. The technology in those things is really amazing. It uses magnetic fields to heat the entire inner pot evenly, not just a heating plate at the bottom. I ended up buying one for my kitchen after reading all the technical specs. It makes the most incredible, perfectly fluffy rice. You have to wash the short-grain rice first, though, until the water runs completely clear. A lot of people skip that step because they're in a hurry, but it removes the excess surface starch. If you don't wash it, the rice gets all gummy and clumps together. 

My grandmother used to use this special bamboo strainer to wash rice when I was a kid. She had this whole technique where she'd swirl the water exactly five times before draining it. She was incredibly particular about cooking in general. She used to spend all Sunday just making these rich, complex broths from scratch, simmering bones for hours and hours... 

Wait, I'm sorry, I lost my train of thought. What did you ask me about the files?

None of the symptom profiles specifically address the patient's interactions with people outside of work regarding the delusion, nor do they detail the reactions of family or friends to the specific evidence.

patient.answer:
Show the files to someone outside of work? No, no, I haven't done that. I haven't talked to a lawyer or anything. For one thing, we have very strict NDAs—non-disclosure agreements. As a translator, you sign them constantly because you're often dealing with sensitive, pre-release material. 

I translated a massive batch of patents last year for this Japanese tech firm, actually. They were designing a new type of induction rice cooker. The technology in those things is really amazing. It uses magnetic fields to heat the entire inner pot evenly, not just a heating plate at the bottom. I ended up buying one for my kitchen after reading all the technical specs. It makes the most incredible, perfectly fluffy rice. You have to wash the short-grain rice first, though, until the water runs completely clear. A lot of people skip that step because they're in a hurry, but it removes the excess surface starch. If you don't wash it, the rice gets all gummy and clumps together. 

My grandmother used to use this special bamboo strainer to wash rice when I was a kid. She had this whole technique where she'd swirl the water exactly five times before draining it. She was incredibly particular about cooking in general. She used to spend all Sunday just making these rich, complex broths from scratch, simmering bones for hours and hours... 

Wait, I'm sorry, I lost my train of thought. What did you ask me about the files?

inference.note: Patient demonstrates persistent delusional belief about file tampering despite repeated contradictory evidence (IT audit trail clean, HR/supervisor dismissal). Unable to provide concrete evidence when directly challenged. Tangential speech with flight of ideas is prominent but secondary to fixed false belief system. No hallucinations or mood disturbance. Meets criteria for Delusional Disorder, Persecutory Type (F22.0) rather than F22.9. F22.9 ruled out as diagnosis is sufficiently specific.

opening_question.intent: Establish rapport and identify the chief complaint that brings the patient to the clinic today
opening_question.question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to see me?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a persistent, systematized delusional belief system centered on workplace file tampering lasting 11 months. Key diagnostic features include: (1) a non-bizarre, encapsulated delusion of reference and persecution involving specific colleagues and subcontractors allegedly altering files to sabotage the patient's work; (2) complete absence of hallucinations or other psychotic symptoms; (3) preserved functioning in other life domains; (4) logical reasoning within the delusional framework; (5) no mood episodes; (6) normal affect and speech organization aside from tangentiality. The patient maintains the delusion despite contradictory evidence (IT audit trail) and resists alternative explanations, even from trusted individuals. This constellation is consistent with Delusional Disorder, Persecutory Type (F22.0). The marked tangentiality and flight of ideas, while present, do not meet criteria for a mood disorder or ADHD, and occur within the context of a fixed delusional system rather than representing primary thought disorder.
